newsitem.title: CHINA: China unfazed by slump in foreign investment vows.
newsitem.headline: China unfazed by slump in foreign investment vows.

text.p: Contracted overseas investment in China slid 49.56 percent in the first half of 1997, but the dramatic thinning of the ranks of foreigners pledging funds has left Beijing unfazed, officials and analysts said on Wednesday.

China approved the creation of 9,763 foreign-invested ventures in the first six months of the year, down 30 percent compared with the same period of 1996, officials of the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation (MOFTEC) said.
Total contracted investment plummeted 49.56 percent to $22.934 billion, they said.
"This kind of fall is normal," MOFTEC spokesman Hu Zhaoqing told a news conference. "It cannot be said that this is an issue of having already reached the (investment) peak.
"There has been a fall in the number of new foreign-invested enterprises deals signed and in the amount of contracted investment... but actual investment has grown," Hu said.
Realised foreign investment rose a year-on-year 5.35 percent in the first half to $20.721 billion, he said, adding that the fall in pledges was the natural result of recent policy shifts.

Beijing had already moved to make consumption a driving force for economic growth and had not been taken by surprise by the slide in contracted investment, said John Seel, sovereign analyst at Bear Stearns Asia Ltd in Hong Kong.
"I do think it's going to slow their growth, but I don't think it's really going to threaten their growth," he said.

China last year withdrew tax privileges on imports of capital goods for foreign-funded ventures, and Hu cited such policies along with a tight monetary policy as reasons for the fall in investment pledges.

The state had prevented a decline in actual investment through transitional policies that softened negative effects for investors with funds already contracted, while new investors would in time adjust to the new rules, he said.

"I think the foreign investors need time to get used to them," he said, adding that China would continue to grant favourable conditions for investment in certain industrial sectors and in economically-backward western regions.

Chinese economists said in June they expected actual foreign investment, 80 percent of which is concentrated in eastern coastal provinces, to decline to around $40 billion this year from a record $42.35 billion in 1996.
Contracted investment fell to $73.21 billion last year from $91.28 billion in 1995 and a record $111.44 billion the year before, the economists said.

While the speed of the first half slide in contracted investment has raised eyebrows and is expected to hit overall economic growth, Chinese and foreign analysts said domestic funds for investment remained relatively plentiful.
"The saving rate is still very high... and the shortage of cash is not as severe as it has been in the last few years," said one economist at a MOFTEC research institute.
The effects of falling foreign investment would be limited, said the economist, who declined to be identified.

A tremendous expansion in production capacity had left few large-scale opportunities available to foreigners in China, but continuing interest abroad meant the decline in investment pledges was likely to slow, said Seel of Bear Stearns.
